The Italian stream frog (Rana italica) is a small-bodied amphibian endemic to the Italian peninsula, and recent field surveys have provided detailed measurements of its life history traits. Adult males achieve a maximum snout–vent length of 7.5 centimeters [Li = 7.5 centimeters], a value consistent with those reported for other stream-dwelling ranids of similar body plan. Females also reach an ultimate SVL of 7.5 centimeters [Li = 7.5 centimeters], indicating a lack of pronounced sexual size dimorphism in this species. At birth, the newly hatched tadpoles emerge from their gelatinous egg masses at a wet weight of just 0.0031 grams [Wwb = 0.0031 grams], a diminutive starting mass that reflects the relatively small egg diameter of 1.5 to 2.1 millimeters documented in this ranid. This neonatal mass places the species at the lower end of the range observed among European brown frogs, likely constraining early larval growth rates and demanding rapid acquisition of exogenous food resources following yolk absorption.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of this species' montane stream habitats (10 °C [T = 10 °C]), the onset of exogenous feeding occurs at approximately 40 days [ab = approximately 40 days] after hatching. At this age, the yolk sac is fully resorbed and the tadpole begins actively grazing on periphyton and detritus, marking the transition from endotrophic to exotrophic nutrition. The larval period is relatively protracted, with metamorphosis occurring after approximately 91.5 days  since birth at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This duration, measured at a constant 10 °C [T = 10 °C], is consistent with the slow developmental pace typical of cool-water breeding anurans. The accelerated body plan reorganisation during metamorphic climax involves tail resorption, limb development, and skin keratinisation, culminating in the emergence of a terrestrial juvenile froglet.

Sexual maturity in the Italian stream frog is reached after approximately 1095 days [tp = approximately 1095 days] since birth, a delayed maturation that reflects the energetic demands of achieving the adult body size of 101 grams [Wwi = 101 grams] in both sexes at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Females attain the same ultimate wet weight as males (101 grams) [Wwi = 101 grams], consistent with the absence of sexual size dimorphism noted for the species. This adult mass, measured under controlled laboratory conditions, situates Rana italica among the medium-sized members of the family Ranidae. Puberty is accompanied by the onset of gonadal activity and gametogenesis, leading to the first amplexus events recorded in late spring following the accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves.

Once sexually mature, females produce a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], a relatively low reproductive frequency typical of montane stream frogs. Each clutch contains approximately 903 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch contains approximately 903 eggs], deposited as a gelatinous egg mass attached to submerged vegetation. The annual reproductive output of approximately 903 eggs per year, derived from the product of clutch size and frequency, is finely tuned to the cool, stable thermal regime of the species' stream habitats at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This fecundity is comparable to that of the congeneric Rana dalmatina, which also produces large clutches under similar thermal conditions, underscoring a conserved reproductive strategy among European brown frogs adapted to lotic environments.

Longevity records for the Italian stream frog indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3285 days [am = approximately 3285 days] under the cool thermal conditions of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This extended lifespan, exceeding nine years, is remarkable for a small anuran and likely reflects the reduced metabolic demands of a low-temperature, stable environment coupled with relatively low predation pressure in montane headwater streams. The combination of delayed maturation, moderate fecundity, and extended reproductive lifespan positions Rana italica along a slow life-history continuum, contrasting with short-lived, high-fecundity anuran species from warmer, more variable habitats.
